blocks.x: Okay, it's going now. Let's get your right name down.
Henry Glass.
And what people call you?
Henry Glass, better know him by Booker T.
Ah, I see. Well, let's see. Today is May the 19th, 1972.
May the 10th. I made 91.
You made 91 on May the 10th? May the 10th. Ah, well, congratulations.
We did in Washington.
Oh, yeah? What were you doing up there?
Playing.
Oh, just... Oh, I didn't get everybody else's name. Go ahead, ladies. Speak up. So they'll know who's talking. Mrs. Bernadine Glass Zarders. Ah.
What did you find out last night?
No, no, it's been in a... I got a write-up on it and everything.
Yeah, so we know he got to play our play. Well, you have to tell Percy ahead of time so he can't... Percy, no, Percy, no. I didn't fix that up with Percy last night.

Oh, yeah. I got the second reel on... Let's see, today is April 19, 1972. We were talking about working on the riverfront, so you... You teamed up with the white fellows? Oh, yeah, yeah, we worked together. That was our gang, you know? Did you have any kind of segregation in those days?
No, no, no. That's all lately, huh? All lately, that come up. No, we didn't have no segregation. The whites and the colors were together. Screw them.
When did you play music?
I used to play music in there, between then.
You mean you'd work on the docks in the daytime or play at night?

Yeah, play at night in the ballrooms and things, you know, we'd have... Most all the ballrooms had bands and things on Fridays and Saturdays and Sundays they'd have bands. But we'd team up and play there. We started playing with three pieces in some of them places. Then they'd have piano. We'd work out with the piano. Yeah, we'd have piano. Piano, drum, and trumpet. Papa Celeste used to work with me. We used to play for Litchens on Edward Street. For Litchens? Litchens. And Almarayston. Oh, Litchens didn't ever tell you about me for years.
Almarayston, you're talking about that play? Sure. I used to play at the Plum Plan. Oh yeah? I played at the Plum Plan. Why did they call it the Plum Plan? I don't know.
That was Peter's Corner.

Well that was the American Legion dance hall when I went there, but they still called it the Plum Plan. Yeah, it used to be the Plum Plan. It was before. Yeah. They changed it to the American Legion hall when we took it and played it when they built it over. You see, they remodeled it. Well I never saw any plums or apples or cherries or pears or anything like that.
Yeah. It's a funny name. Plum Plan? Plum Plan. It used to call it. Oh. Then the American Legion moved, they moved back to Franklin Avenue on that.
By the overpass. They moved up in there. Though we used to be right there at Claiborne and Music. Yeah, Claiborne and Music. That's the one I used to do.
Yeah. They had Buck Vanville's band there for years. Yeah. The Philly Red. You remember Philly Red? Yeah. You remember Philly Red? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. I heard of them. Yeah. Yeah. I heard of them. Phil and Ray, Bill Gallaty. Mm-hmm. All them fellas used to, we used to buck together on the lake. Which Bill Gallaty? Bill Gallaty, he used to play bass.
Oh yeah, not the young man today that plays trumpet. Yeah.

One played trumpet and one used to play the bass. And Philly Ray used to play bass. We used to get on the lake and buck out there. The camps would be right there, side and side. We used to get there and blow at each other. Dixon Land.
You're talking about humpback Gallaty though. Yeah.

The Dixon Land man. That's why we played. They used to play the music that we play now. Yeah. And we'd buck on the lake every Sunday. We'd go out there on a Saturday night. That's where the money stopped. Start the raise and you know the price.
Is that the area they used to call Meilenburg? The Meilenburg.

Meilenburg. Meilenburg. Yeah. More Road, we'd be out there playing for More Road and then we'd be in all them camp playing across from each other. We used to buck. Bill Gallaty, he ain't long died. He old. All of them dying. Philly Ray. Old timers, you know. Sharky, he left. Sharky used to be out there. We used to be, me and Sharky used to talk about you. Sharky used to say, Glass, you still living you old rascal. We used to be, oh, me and Sharky, that'd be like that. Well you used to mix it up? Yeah, we used to buck out there on the lake. Yeah. Yeah, we used to buck out there. The camp, this camp here, we'd be right there. We'd be blowing at each other. Yeah, we used to play that music out there. Every sudden we'd go on the boat and play, the camellial. Yeah, the boat used to go across the lake. across the lake. They called it the Camellia. Did it go along the canal and get the lake? It'd go across, it'd bring you across the lake and it'd come back in the evening and trip. The Camellia boat. Where did it leave from? It leave from right out there on the wharf by Littlefield Street there. The train would go out on the wharf, a punching train. She'd roll right on out to the wharf and get off the hood. End of the wharf. And that little excursion train would go out there? She'd be clear on, she'd leave at the junction up there. Littlefield and the kid up there. But that's where the punching train used to be. That she'd back up and come back and go to Millen Boy. And that's where we'd get that train and go out there and flip. Sometimes we'd be out there all night on a Saturday and Sunday we'd be out there on picnets, you know. They'd have them in camp. Play all night and all day out there. We'd be bucking. The white band and the colored band. They were always like that. They didn't have that pulling in the hall like they were doing, you know. They was all like that. They'd come up that way. The colored would stay next door to you, they'd hand you something to dinner over there. My grandmother would hand the white people something over there. That's the way they got along, long time ago. They didn't, they didn't, they didn't pull in the hall. They'd pull in the hall and this come up at the time of the young race. It wasn't like that. They'd give you anything they had. And if you were sick they'd come in that house and stay there with you because some of your people would come. They'd have to mind you. And they'd wash you. They'd have to wash you. They used to come and help to wash the colored people when they died, the women. They'd come and help you. So this would change what I was used to that, you see. And I'm a little tired down now because everything is changed now. Yes, it must be very different. Yeah. They just got you that you could go anywhere. So they'd give you anything you had. They'd reach you and hand you your dinner, your coffee. Did I show if you had coffee? You know? And this broke away gradually. Now this is the same as
the whole thing. How did Dee used to play with you? I never heard you mention your

username. Who? Dee Dee. Well Dee Dee and Billy, well they know, you didn't know Dee Dee and Billy, but they started with me. Billy and Dee Dee was rehearsing at my house. That's where they started. Oh yeah? Billy and Dee Dee started right at my house. They practiced every day. It was Sunday. Billy and Dee Dee lived at my house. They'd sleep by my house and everything. Billy and Dee Dee. You played with Mr. Bucko Grammer? Bucko Grammer, Dijama, Gagne. I'm about to see to get them bitches. Yeah, I like seeing. Yeah, Bucko Grammer, Dijama. You played with Albert Francis? He played in the band too. Albert Francis. I played with all them fellas which live and now I've been playing with them. I've seen some of them young. You know, small. Albert Francis. Did you ever know Sidney Bechet? Yeah, Sidney Bechet was a young boy. Sidney Bechet left young. Sidney Bechet learned on the flute. Sidney Bechet used to be by my house. Paul Barnes learned on the flute. Paul Barnes. He learned on the flute.
A little tin flute? Yeah, tin flute. Paul Barnes learned how to play that. How much did those flutes cost then? We used to pay ten cents for them.

Ten cents. Ten cents. When you get a big one, they charge you fifty cents for a big one. They find out they were playing music with. They charge you fifty cents. I have a flute home where we used to play in the band. It's plastic. I got one of the plastic. I got it home. I got all my skulls home when I used to use on the drums. Car bells. Four car bells used to use. Triangles. I got all that home. Them fellas didn't use them. They used triangles and other things? Yeah, we had triangles. I got one home. They don't use that. We had four car bells used to hook on the drums. We'd play on them car bells. Play a song on them car bells. You have to take your heart on that car bell. That rhythm, you know? That drum had to make his part on that rhythm. What about the skulls? What were they like then? Just like the four skeleton heads. I have that home. Temple blocks, that's what they call them. I've seen them there. I got all that home. Tum Tum. I got one of them old Tum Tums.
Charny Tum Tums. Well how old was Bechet when he started playing?

Oh Bechet was a young man. Bechet left. I was staying on Malibu Street and Bechet left. That's Wooden Joe's relation, Sidney Bechet. He sent Wooden Joe his client from away. Wooden Joe had client heads. That's Wooden Joe's uncle I believe, Bechet. Sidney Bechet. He wasn't as old as Wooden Joe. Oh no. His nephew. His nephew. Yeah. No he wasn't as old as Joe. And we got Paul, Paul, Bonds had some brothers, Boos, they was playing. Paul Bonds. And Mealy Bonds' uncle. What did Boos play? Boos was playing Clownet. Who did he play with? I never knew. He played with the Camellia Band too. He played with the Camellia Band. He used to play with us. I knew Mealy played but I never knew anything

about him playing. Yeah. He played. He used to play at the Plum playing with us. That's funny. I never did know anything about him as well as I know him. Yeah Boos. Oh one more thing about the riverfront. Did you ever see anybody down there playing any music?

On the river? Yeah. Well they had a lot of mandrains out there playing music. Like guitars? Yes. They were guitars. They'd sing. They'd go around singing around the bottom of the world, guitar. And they was playing. That's with their band, you see. Some of them were blues singers. A lot of them was playing music. It wasn't like us was playing in the band, you know a band. There'd be three of them going together to the guitar, violin and a chorus. And that's why they played. They had bands there. They'd go out there in the ballroom and they'd be out there. They'd have them out there in the French Quarter.

Would they have them on the riverfront too, the same guys? By the ballroom down there. Yeah they used to work out there. So they were sidelined, you know. Oh I see. I thought maybe when you'd be working, maybe during lunch hour they'd have something
like that. No, no, no, no. The sidelined when they'd be off. That was the hustle, you know.
Oh I see. Yeah, that was the hustle. You ever know any mandolin players? I know a lot of them. Bob, Bob. He stayed on

Sun Rock Street. I don't know if you didn't know Bob. He stayed right there, Sun Rock Cross from the graveyard. The Sun Rock graveyard. I don't remember anybody named Bob that played mandolin. No, he used to play mandolin and he played violin.

I can't place him. Yeah. Bob. Did you know Chicken Binks? I know Chicken. Was he very good? He was good. Yeah, he was good. Well what was your very first music job that you ever played? Playing at the Plunk Plant. I was playing at the Plunk Plant.

That was your first job? Then I went to play for the Judd City Burser. We used to play. You see Garnier used to be the leader of the band and he died and I took the band over. And we played for the brothers. I can play in all them jobs. So that made me be the leader. That's the way we'd take it. When a member would die in the band, the other fellow would take over and wanted to take over. And then the other one would join in with us. So most every man you see out there done been a leader of a band. Jim Crow, all of them. They done been leaders of the band. That's why they can get together and they know that's what they're going to do.
But how old were you when you started playing music, Bob?

I started playing music when I was about twenty. Oh, about twenty? Yeah, I was young. Yeah, because they had to take and bring me around. They had to come around and ask for the little need. Were you wearing long pants? They were running in long pants, I'm going to tell you the truth. The policemen run me in long pants. We were the men. They were the runners in long pants.
What do you mean they run you in long pants?

We didn't run away long pants, they were the men. Oh, I see. The policemen, long time ago, when you get to be twenty or eighteen, nineteen, like that, they run you in long pants. You had to be a man. Because we'd be doing men's work. In the policemen class, they said, they're men. They'd run us. We had to get in long pants. We were great big fellas, so we were men's. They run you every time you catch it. They whip you on the leg with that strap on his clout.
Yeah.
Yeah, they run this and all that. You remember Garnier, the gentleman.
I never did know the gentleman Garnier. I'm going to get his picture for you. I never met him.
This was my daddy's picture. Let me get in there.
Yeah, I got your suit on and everything. You see the shoes. Oh!
Yeah, these runners, they're running. I'll be back. Listen, watch yourself, folks. I'm going to jump over there. I can see. Now, you take a walk now.
Uh-uh, don't you go far left.
I ain't go far. That's my trouble. I walk into everything.

I walk from here to the house down there and back here again today. And he does that every day. Uh-huh. Unless he's staying here today. You got to keep him moving. How far is that? My Jiggy Street is about a mile from here. Oh, that's nothing for him. But I worry about him, you see, because he's got to go down some stair steps at the overpass, and that's 100 feet up in the head, or stair steps, and he will not catch the bus. You give him a tall path, and I'll be standing in the door, he'll watch me until you see that door close, and then he's going on down the hours. What do you spend that money on?
You got to keep him walking.
He tells me he's been spending for coffee. I got on the bus and I said, I didn't see you catch that bus.
I buy candy, peanuts. Yeah, I eat candy, peanuts. I like kids.
Oh, yeah? Well, what's the longest parade you ever played?
The longest parade? The one from back of St. Minard. The Paris Air Force. That's the longest parade.
Oh, you mean for Mardi Gras?
Yeah. That's the longest parade we got.
How many hours does it take?
Oh, I don't take. We make that in about three hours. From back of Paris Avenue, you know, what's the name of that club? That's DSAC Boulevard.
No, no, no. Endymion. Endymion Club, yeah. Yeah. Well, how long is the Jolly Bunch? Oh, the Jolly Bunch is all day. That's a long parade. I think they start at 12 or 1.
No, they start at 9. They start at 9.
But as them, before they get together. Do you ever play for eight hours on a parade? I've played plenty of times. Yeah, we done played more than eight hours.

Yeah, we done played more than eight hours. Yeah, you can see that. When we leave the parade, we go into places and play. In the bar room, we go into the bar room and they don't want to leave us go. They should have to pay extra money and we play there. Yeah. Sometimes we meet until four o'clock. Then we leave and go by bus to play. Just for kicks then. Just getting kicks out of it. Enjoy it. We go by bus then.
What book when you was playing with the Jefferson City Buzzards?
Oh, we worked all day.
It was called out at eight o'clock.
Yeah. No, seven o'clock. Seven o'clock. Seven o'clock to Jefferson City Buzzards.
And you didn't get back until after six.
After six in the evening. Well, that's a long parade. Yeah, that's a long parade too, the Jefferson City Buzzards. We used to go to the Buzzards Roofs. That used to be the Buzzards Roofs.
Up on around the... Yeah, the Ottoman Park.

Annunciation and the St. Andrews. Yeah, we'd go up there. We had to leave for six o'clock. Did you come down close to the canal? We'd go all the way to Canal Street. We'd make Canal Street. I didn't figure that way long. I enjoyed it. With Mr. Marks. They got my picture up in their club. Oh yeah?
The Jefferson City Buzzard, Mr. Marks.

They all took a liking to me. See when Ghani died I took over. The Chameleon Band. And you go up there now and you'll see the Chameleon Band. They got it up there. I played for the Eleonora Club. I played for all of them club. How many stops would you make? Oh we'd make stops. They had plenty stops. They had a lot of stops.
That's why you don't feel them.

Them stops taking it all because they've been bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo That's why you don't feel it. Them stops take it off. Because they be enjoying, they be drinking and eating you. You ain't feeling that. I don't feel it. I go play them parades and I'm feeling it and I don't feel it.

Have you ever been to a parade here like that Sandy, where they make stops and everything? Do you know what they're doing? I've only heard of that. We be drinking and going on. They go in the ballrooms? Yeah. And they get free beer.
They have sandwiches and everything. Then some of the men have it by the house. You be stopping all the way along. Then they be eating and drinking.
They'll get pretty drunk by the end of the parade.
Oh, some of them get drunk far out. Some of them fall out.
I remember Pete Fountain won Mardi Gras. He carried the last mile. His toes just kind of making a little vague motions down there. That's the guy on each side holding him up.

Well Sharky and all them fellas used to be out there praying and Sharky and them. We all been together like that. Me and Sharky and them used to be like that. Did you play in the same band with Sharky ever? No. We used to buck together all the time. Just buck? Yeah. We'd get kicks at each other. We'd be blowing at each other. Holding our own drinks out to them. Sometimes they wouldn't be drinking and we'd be drinking.
Yeah.
And they'd be looking at us. We'd be making fun at them. We'd get kicks out there. The train going there and the walk.
I want to show you my elephant dog.
You remember?
The dog? My elephant dog.

Bob Woodley and Tati and Warner, there was three brothers. And they had a band used to go around the French market and they used to play. One played bass, one played ghetto, another played violin. And they used to go all around the French market and play in the ballroom and things. Tati, huh? Tati. They had Tati, Warner and Bob. They were three brothers. Well who played the violin? Tati. I heard of it. Yeah, Tati. And Warner would play bass and he played at caudon. They had a caudon. They had a caudon. I don't know who's got that picture. I seen them. I'm trying to get them pictures for you. I'm going to get Ghanese pictures for you. I'm going to get the jammer.
What was their last name, Tati?

I just don't know about Tati and Warner. I used to know their whole name. All their people died out. Now I got to just misplace them, you know. They got away, because they all were born from Pintler House and St. Sophie and things like that. They were from down the river these days? Yeah, down the river. They were from St. Sophie and Pintler House.

Did you ever know a guy named Warner Reed? Warner, I knew it more. What did he play? He used to play banjo. Oh I see. Who was he with? He used to play with the Hornwood band. Oh, we were going to ask him about Buddy Bowling.

Buddy Bowling, I don't know that. Buddy Bowling used to play around there. He used to be around playing the street. Thought I heard Buddy Bowling say, funky boy, funky boy, take it away. I knew him. He used to play around the front of Decatur Street. Decatur Street. Yeah, he used to be all around in there. There used to be ballroom bands. Buddy Bowling and them. Warner, Tateek and them, they would get together. That was their big band.
Oh, they'd make a big band?
Make a big band out of it. They started getting together after all the other bands was making up. My nephew Howard Mandorf, he ain't long died. Yeah.
Yeah, Howard. Was Buddy Bowling really a great ladies' man? He was good. He was good. I don't mean as a musician, but I understand he was really a ladies' man.
All of them old timers used to be lovers. Did they? Yeah, all the old timers used to be lovers because I used to be a lover.
There you go.
Sure, I used to be a lover. I'm still a lover, yeah.
That goes with the music, huh?
Yeah, the musicians. Show me a musician who don't like the ladies. Yeah, I guess so. Every musician. If he don't be standing by the ladies, he's going to come behind.
But only one at a time, huh, Buck? No worries. I mean, now, now you only have-
Now, now, yeah, I only got one friend. Before I had three boys. I was a runner. Say that again. She said, say that again. Yeah, I was a runner.
He even took his alligator in the ballroom. You took your alligator in the ballroom? Yeah, Pete. I had an alligator. Who did you name your alligator after?

Pete. Yeah, I named him Pete. I had a duck before the jets come out. Before the jet plane come out, I had a duck born just like a jet. Oh, yeah? And the collector wanted to buy that duck. He come home, he wanted to give my wife $10 for it. Right where I'm staying there in the yard. That duck would walk around here just like a jet. Then them jet planes come out. And he wanted to give it $10 for it and we wouldn't sell it to him. He got it to next corner. The dog broke the duck neck. I couldn't do nothing for him because he was kicking. I had a little black dog. I had a little black dog. He was short legs and he was about that long. I forget how they called him. They gave him to me. That little dog made, two dogs made an elephant.
They made an elephant?
Two dogs made an elephant. I got that here.
You bred him and you still got the elephant?
The elephant died. You see I was away, where I went to here? We went away, where we went boy? Boy?
You was up there in the seven row drinking. And when you come back, the dog has been embalmed. You're embalmed.
Yeah, well I embalmed him by a meal.
He looked like an elephant?
Yeah, he was a LeBron took a LeBron involved.
And he's looking at me but he's not sheep.
I know, I know it so.
I've heard about it.

Yeah, look, two dogs made that elephant. I took him, when I came back from playing music, the dog had died. If I had listened to my little grandson, I went into that house and I was rushing to go play music. Yeah, it looks like an elephant. So we got him there. That's it. The back is the dog. Two dogs made an elephant.
Oh yeah. He's got a nose like an elephant. Did you ever see that? You see the snoot under there?
Yeah.
You see the snoot?
And he was the only boy, but he was stamped from Board of Health. Yeah.

I done been all over with it. There was plenty of money with that dog. I'm here. That's a barman fluid. You see they got this. Yeah, the middle of the body involved. Well I don't let daddy and them keep this dog at all. No, cause some of them fellas get drunk and they drop it. How long did he live?
He lived for three.
March the 17th, 1954, and he died March the 20th, 1954.
Three days. Yeah, I was a winner.
I was a winner. You know, I was a winner. You know, I was a winner.
You know, I was a winner.
You know, I was a winner.
You know, I was a winner.
You know, I was a winner. You know, I was a winner. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.

And they got that little girl at the Cathedral Church. That's supposed to be my baby. At the Cathedral Church? At the Cathedral Church, a little black baby. It's in the Cathedral Church and they moved that from St. Rock Graveyard. Called Leona. Mama took and went to Fish Fry and come back home and give her the breast. And she died of poison. That was my little baby from St. Rock Graveyard. The fella showed me the baby. Though they moved it. He told me, he said they're going to move your baby. He used to work there. They called him English. See we all used to stay right there. I used to play in that St. Rock Graveyard. They didn't have no fence around. They used to be where we played. You see that St. Rock Street, we took and fixed that with garbage. I worked for every one of the ward leaders. When one would die, they didn't put me with that one. With the winners. You know, I'd drive every one of the ward leaders. When the husband died, I'd drive the city wagon. And I used to win the prize every year. We'd have to have inspections for them garbage cars. I didn't pick up nothing but paper and stuff. Oyster shells around the place. And we, that St. Rock Street is nothing but garbage. You filled it in with garbage? I filled it all the way from the market, all the way around to Franklin Avenue. That's all garbage. We'd cut many horses, mules, they'd fall on and bog up in it and they'd cut their, they'd have to kill them, you know. They'd have to come in and kill them. All that's garbage.
That playground, St. Rock Playground is garbage. What about Buddy Bowling some more? Did you know any of the guys that he played with?
Well, some of the fellas I didn't know. Coke or beer, anybody?
No, thanks. Make some water if you got any water.
Bye, Buddy.
Coke would suit me.
Bye, Buddy.

No, I didn't play with Buddy Bowling. I didn't play with him. Cause they had their line up. They played. And you knew the guys in his band? Did you know any of them? I just know them by seeing them, you know, the part being friends with them like that,
you know.
We was always on a go with our little hustle.
Oh, I see.

But he was good. He was, he was working, he was working regularly now. Cause he always kept a job that he could go. He always had somebody, somebody hiring him. He was working. And Buddy Bowling was a good band. That's for entertaining and different things like that. They were good. Where did Buddy Bowling die? Was that down here in New Orleans or? I wouldn't know where he died. I believe he died in here in New Orleans.
Do you remember when they took him off to jail and to the hospital and all that? Were you around then?
No. No I wasn't.
I've heard all kinds of stories about him.
Bigfoot Willis.
They had Bigfoot Willis.

Who was he? That was the fellow. He used to play a flute. He used to wear a cape. He was a great big tall black fella. He looked like a big elephant. And he had Bigfoot. They called him Bigfoot Willis. And he used to go around and blow a flute around Decatur Street.
How did you get your nickname, Booker T?

Dr. Tudry raised me. Dr. Tudry raised me. Dr. Tudry raised me. Dr. Tudry raised me. I used to drive him around the horse and buggy. You see, a long time ago we didn't have no automobiles. They didn't have no automobiles. But I used to drive him around the horse and buggy. Sometimes he'd be out there one, two o'clock in the morning before he could get around to your house. So he'd make all that route. And I used to drive him in a horse and buggy. He still, his son is living. I believe his son was, his son Tudry. Dr. Tudry, I believe Dr. Tudry's graduated from LSU. Dr. Tudry is on Roman Street. He's on Roman Street. He's still on Roman Street. He lost his sight. Ralph Tudry. They got Ralph Tudry and Roy Tudry. When Ralph Tudry was playing music out there somewhere in the French Quarter, he'd be looking for me. He didn't know me. He'd have forgotten me. It's been so long. And when he'd hear us say I'm playing out there, he'd be ringing his brother. And Ralph and Dr. Tudry doctored me. He brought me up to a big man. He called you Booker T? He named me Booker T. That's the man who gave me that name. Booker T. Washington. Never tell a lie. Because I'd get out there. I'd be beating them boys up, you know. The little vex. The little vex. They used to stay across the street. And I was the only scholars fellow who used to be at Claiborne. He used to be here. dear
Booker T. Booker T, yeah. Booker T. We got the third reel on there, Buck, but we never did get about how Big Eye Louie got his nickname.

We named him Big Eye Louie. Playing in the band. When he'd get mad, you know, and we didn't ask for a number, and one of them would make a humbug, Louie would open up Big Eye, and Johnny Pedro would say, look at that Big Eye Rabbit. Big Eye Rabbit? Big Eye Rabbit. He used to call Big Eye Louie. He belonged to the child in the living room. Yeah. Big Eye Louie, all of them used to be .

segments.title: Opening: name, date and chatter before the second reel
segments.summary: Interviewer gets Glass's name and nickname Booker T., the date, and the names of others in the room; some side talk.

segments.title: Working the riverfront with white men; no segregation
segments.summary: Second reel resumes on riverfront work. Glass says Black and white worked together and segregation came only lately.

segments.title: Docks by day, playing ballrooms at night
segments.summary: Glass played piano, drum and trumpet trios in ballrooms on weekends while working the docks, with Papa Celestin and for Litchens.

segments.chapter: Bands, lake camps and early players
segments.title: The Plum Plan hall, later the American Legion hall
segments.summary: Talk about the Plum Plan dance hall, its name, its remodeling into the American Legion hall, and its location.

segments.chapter: Bands, lake camps and early players
segments.title: Bucking the white bands at the lake camps and the Camellia boat
segments.summary: Glass recalls bucking with Gallaty, Philly Ray and Sharkey at Milneburg camps, the Camellia boat and excursion train, and how Black and white neighbors once got along.

segments.chapter: Bands, lake camps and early players
segments.title: Dee Dee and Billy, Bucko Grammer, Albert Francis and young Bechet
segments.summary: Glass says Dee Dee and Billy started rehearsing at his house and lists men he played with, including Sidney Bechet as a boy.

segments.chapter: Bands, lake camps and early players
segments.title: Tin flutes and old drum equipment
segments.summary: Prices of tin flutes and Glass's old drum gear: car bells, triangles, temple blocks and tum-tums.

segments.chapter: Bands, lake camps and early players
segments.title: Bechet and Wooden Joe, and the Bonds brothers
segments.summary: Bechet's age and relation to Wooden Joe, plus Paul Bonds, Boos and Mealy Bonds, who played in the Camellia Band.

segments.chapter: Bands, lake camps and early players
segments.title: Street and riverfront musicians: guitars, violin, mandolin
segments.summary: Glass describes string bands and singers who hustled around the riverfront and French Quarter, and a mandolin player named Bob.

segments.chapter: Bands, lake camps and early players
segments.title: First job at the Plum Plan; taking over the Garnier band
segments.summary: Glass's first job was at the Plum Plan; when leader Garnier died he took over the band, a common succession.

segments.chapter: Bands, lake camps and early players
segments.title: Starting music at about twenty; policemen and long pants
segments.summary: Glass began playing around twenty and explains that police treated young men as men once they wore long pants.

segments.chapter: Bands, lake camps and early players
segments.title: Garnier's picture and family chatter about Glass's walks
segments.summary: Photos of Garnier and a relative's father, then relatives talking about Glass's daily walks and habits.

segments.title: The longest Mardi Gras parades and playing after them
segments.summary: Glass names the longest parades, how many hours they last, and how bands play in bars afterward.

segments.title: Jefferson City Buzzards parade, stops and drinking
segments.summary: Glass describes all-day Buzzards parades, taking over the Camellia Band after Garnier died, club stops and the free food and drink.

segments.title: Bucking with Sharkey and other parade musicians; elephant dog interruption
segments.summary: Glass says he and Sharkey never played together but bucked and joked in parades; talk drifts to the elephant dog.

segments.title: Tati, Warner and Bob, three brothers' French Market band
segments.summary: Glass recalls three brothers who played bass, guitar and violin around the French Market; he cannot recall their last name.

segments.title: Warner Reed and Buddy Bolden's ballroom bands
segments.summary: Interviewer asks about banjoist Warner Reed and Buddy Bolden, who played around Decatur Street; Glass says some players combined into a big band.

segments.title: Musicians and the ladies
segments.summary: Glass and the interviewers joke that old-time musicians were all lovers, himself included.

segments.title: Pete the alligator, the duck and the two-dog elephant
segments.summary: Glass tells of his pet alligator Pete, a jet-like duck and a stuffed dog that looks like an elephant, with dates of its life.

segments.title: The baby moved from St. Roch graveyard and Glass's garbage-wagon work
segments.summary: Glass speaks of his baby Leona's grave and his job driving the city garbage wagon that filled in St. Roch Street.

segments.title: More on Buddy Bolden, and Bigfoot Willis the flute player
segments.summary: Asked about Bolden's band, Glass says he knew them only by sight; Bolden worked regularly and Glass was not around when he was taken away. Glass also describes Bigfoot Willis, a tall flutist in a cape on Decatur Street.

segments.title: How Glass got the name Booker T. from Dr. Tudry
segments.summary: Glass was raised by Dr. Tudry, drove his horse and buggy, and was given the name Booker T. by him.

segments.title: Third reel: how Big Eye Louie got his nickname
segments.summary: Glass explains the band nicknamed Louie Big Eye because he opened his eyes wide when angry.
